Organize your latte station so everything's within easy reach—making it simple to keep up your healthy coffee habit. Instant Latte for On-the-Go: Packing and Enjoying Anywhere One of the best parts about instant latte packets? You can take them anywhere! Whether you're headed to work, the gym, or an outdoor adventure, they're easy to pack and prepare. Just bring your favorite travel mug, instant latte packet, and you're ready to go. You can even bring your favorite coffee on a long-haul flight. All you need is hot water and you're set for a nourishing, energizing beverage wherever life takes you. Pair with healthy snacks like nuts or fruit for a balanced mini meal that supports your active lifestyle. What is the Coffee Community Saying About Laird Superfood? title: Chasing Yield with DeFi Aggregators
summary: The DeFi space has seen impressive innovation and traction over the last two years. As DeFi continues to evolve, DeFi aggregators are emerging as a strong trend. As user-facing products built on decentralized infrastructure, DeFi aggregators unlock the potential for higher yields and a better user experience.
body_text: The DeFi space has seen impressive innovation and traction over the last two years, with the total value locked in the DeFi ecosystem surpassing $9.4 billion in mid-September ( DeFi Pulse ). As DeFi continues to evolve, DeFi aggregators are emerging as a strong trend. As user-facing products built on decentralized infrastructure, DeFi aggregators unlock the potential for higher yields and a better user experience. Because returns vary greatly across different lending platforms, aggregators help investors get the highest possible yield. Aggregators played a key role in the recent yield farming craze by leveraging DeFi protocols to maximize user returns. While protocols such as Compound, Uniswap, and others have built out user-facing applications, their priority remains centered on core functionality. In contrast, aggregators focus on simplifying and improving the experience for the end user. For example, in the case of an alternative savings account, users don’t need to worry about the underlying smart contracts or networks; instead, they simply deposit money and watch interest accrue. Quantstamp is proud to have helped secure some of the industry’s leading DeFi aggregator projects including Idle Finance, Rari Capital, and Yearn: Idle.Finance Idle Finance is a DeFi rebalancing protocol, which tokenizes the best interest rate across different lending protocols on the Ethereum money market. With Idle, users and dApp developers don’t have to switch funds between lending protocols manually. Instead, by buying and holding IdleTokens, a user’s underlying position is rebalanced dynamically each time the lending protocol that is offering the highest rate changes. This allows users to always attain the most profitable return for their savings. Different allocation strategies can be chosen, allowing users to choose between maximum yield or risk-adjusted. Rari Capital Rari positions themselves as the “Smartest Stable Robo-Advisor,” and is built to maximize yield across protocols such as Compound, Aave, Synthetix, and Curve. Rari lets anyone with an Ethereum-based wallet access the protocol, lend their funds, and participate in what’s known as yield farming. Funds begin earning interest as soon as they are deposited, with a 20% performance fee being deducted from all yield earned by RFT token holders. Yearn.Finance Yearn, a community-driven project, provides a way for liquidity providers to maximize their yield and is intended to be governed in a decentralized manner. After launching their token in July, they experienced unprecedented growth which has shown no signs of slowing down, recently surpassing $900M in Total Value Locked (TVL). Quantstamp worked with the community to provide an informal code review of their Y Pool, Staking, and Governance pools. What’s Next DeFi aggregators are already experiencing product-market fit, so they will likely play a bigger role as the DeFi space continues to develop. By unlocking better yields and providing an unparalleled user experience, aggregators are driving DeFi users to various protocols and supporting even greater adoption within the space.

title: The Evolving Role of the Software Architect
summary: From ivory tower to irreplaceable. Why the Software Architect still anchors every ambitious tech roadmap.
body_text: Software Architecture Principal Engineer Ai Engineering Tech Leadership The Evolving Role of the Software Architect Alexei Krasner 22 min read · Jun 3, 2025 -- In today’s fast-moving tech organizations, the role of the software architect is both misunderstood and more vital than ever. Over the past decade, many companies have moved away from traditional “Software Architect” titles. They now favor Principal Engineers and Staff Engineers as the senior individual contributors guiding technology. (Interestingly, not all companies agree on the seniority of those roles, but I’ll use them as common examples for simplicity.) On the surface, this seems like a semantic change — a simple rebranding. In reality, it reflects deeper cultural shifts in how we approach system design and technical leadership. Yet despite title changes, the need for architectural thinking has not diminished. The business challenges (and product requirements) in the last 10–15 years brought the usage of many emerging technologies/patterns/frameworks/methodologies like Microservices and Event-Driven Architectures, Cloud Computing (with Serverless and Edge), Containerization Orchestration, DevOps/DevSecOps/MLOps (all with large portions of IaC), Big Data and Data Engineering, ML, AI, and many more. This article (or manifesto if you wish) explores the evolving role of software architects in modern organizations, merging theory with hard-won practical lessons. It advocates for an empowered architectural function that addresses complexity, aligns with business strategy, and charts a future-ready path in an age of constant change. Press enter or click to view image in full size From “Architect” to “Principal Engineer”: A Shift in Title, Not Purpose It wasn’t long ago that large technology organizations commonly had designated Software Architects — individuals or teams tasked with defining the system’s architecture and guiding the engineering teams during implementation. However, many companies became wary of this traditional architect role, which was often negatively portrayed as the “ivory tower” architect — someone who created diagrams in isolation and then simply passed them on to the development teams to build. This skepticism was, in some ways, justified. There were many cases where architects became too detached from the everyday realities of coding, leading to designs that were not really practical. In response, companies started to move away from formal architect titles, preferring senior engineers who remained hands-on with the code. The specific title of ‘Architect’ became less prevalent, even though the essential architectural responsibilities continued to be very important and were being fulfilled by engineers at the Staff/Principal levels, expected to balance their coding work with broader system design responsibilities. Having observed this evolution firsthand as a leader, executive, or in prior architecture roles, my viewpoint is one of nuanced appreciation coupled with a degree of caution. On one hand, the renewed emphasis on the engineering discipline within architectural responsibilities has undeniably helped mitigate the pitfalls of overly naive and impractical planning tendencies. This shift has also facilitated a valuable career path for senior technical contributors to assume leadership without becoming detached from the realities of implementation. Conversely, simply altering job titles does not inherently eliminate the fundamental need for dedicated architectural focus. Designating an individual as a Principal Engineer does not automatically confer the requisite time allocation, cross-functional authority, or specialized architectural acumen necessary to effectively address strategic, big-picture architectural concerns. In some organizations, I’ve noted a tendency for the shift to swing excessively in this direction, with “no architects, only engineers” becoming an almost dogmatic principle. This can inadvertently lead to a situation of architecture by committee — or worse, by happenstance — where no single entity is explicitly responsible for considering the broader system design beyond their team or microservice. In most cases, decisions are driven by immediate needs like solution delivery, feature implementation, or specific problem-solving. The potential ramifications of this approach include the development of incoherent systems, the inefficient duplication of efforts across teams, and the eventual necessity for costly and disruptive refactoring initiatives. While I don’t want to overemphasize refactoring as the primary theme here, it serves as a critical downstream impact of a poorly understood architectural function. Engineering teams often struggle to fully connect their past decisions and implemented solutions to the accumulation of debt, making it challenging to track, monitor, and quantify this relationship, especially given the potentially prolonged timeframe between cause and effect. Furthermore, the ability to clearly differentiate between general technical debt and debt that is fundamentally architectural in nature is often lacking, further obscuring the true cost of neglecting dedicated architectural oversight. The core tenet remains that software architecture is fundamentally a function, a continuous set of essential activities, rather than simply a specific rank or title within the organization. Whether we formally designate individuals as ‘Architects,’ ‘Principal Engineers,’ or ‘Staff Developers’ is ultimately a matter of nomenclature. The critical aspect is ensuring that seasoned technical leaders are actively engaged in the process of architectural thinking on a daily basis: considering systems from a comprehensive, holistic viewpoint, making strategic design decisions that have an enduring impact, and providing a clear and compelling technical vision for the future direction of our platforms. In many organizations, the Principal Engineer effectively embodies the role of the software architect for a particular domain, bearing ultimate responsibility for its success and its technical evolution. Senior engineers, including Principal and Staff Engineers, are undoubtedly capable of handling architectural duties and often do so with great proficiency. However, their primary day-to-day responsibilities usually focus on other critical matters, such as leading product initiatives, guiding team execution, and resolving immediate technical challenges. This inherent focus on more immediate concerns can often conflict with the continuity and dedicated focus required for effective and consistent architectural work. Architects, on the other hand, often dedicate a significant portion of their time specifically to these broader architectural considerations, ensuring a continuous and proactive (continuous and proactive are key here) approach rather than addressing them solely as momentary challenges arise. This dedicated focus allows for more consistent systemic thinking, proactive future planning, and effective alignment across disparate teams — a level of sustained attention that can be difficult for even the most capable senior engineers to maintain alongside their other crucial responsibilities. Navigating the Complexity of Modern Distributed Architectures Over the last decade (and a half), software architecture has profoundly changed — not just because new technologies emerged, but because business and product requirements have become more innovative, ambitious, and demanding. Architectures must now inherently support scalability, agility, real-time interactions, personalized user experiences, global distribution, and robust compliance. Architects no longer deal merely with selecting frameworks or organizing code modules; their role is now to strategically manage unprecedented complexity, stitching together diverse technologies and methodologies into coherent systems capable of solving intricate business challenges. To effectively discuss these new aspects, let’s look at three core areas of complexity that modern software architects must handle in large technology-driven companies, taking inspiration from my experience in building platforms for the dynamic world of Sports Betting and iGaming: Distributed Systems and Event-Driven Complexity As products evolve from monolithic applications to highly distributed ecosystems, architects face new challenges around data consistency, latency, event management, and transactional integrity. Patterns like Microservices and Event-Driven Architectures, originally introduced to achieve scalability and autonomy, require architects to adopt entirely new ways of thinking about systems. At DraftKings, for instance, the real-time nature of a Sportsbook involves streaming millions of odds updates per second, triggering events based on user interactions (such as bet placement), and synchronizing state across multiple platforms (mobile apps, web, backend services). Designing such systems isn’t simply about choosing technology — it’s about defining clear boundaries, effective data contracts, and resilient patterns to cope with volatility and unpredictability. Architects must strategically determine how to partition logic, manage eventual consistency, handle fault-tolerance scenarios, and ensure real-time responsiveness. This complexity didn’t originate from technology — it was driven by the innovative business requirement to deliver dynamic, engaging, and real-time user experiences. Infrastructure as Software and Operational Excellence A second layer of complexity arises from how modern systems are deployed, operated, and managed. With practices like DevOps, DevSecOps, MLOps, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC), the responsibility of architects has expanded into what was traditionally considered “operations.” Containerization (Docker) and orchestration platforms (Kubernetes), combined with Cloud Computing and serverless platforms, by far not an exhaustive list, now allow rapid development and deployment but also introduce greater intricacy in configuration, security, and observability. Consider an example: launching an operation in a newly regulated market at DraftKings involves not just building the product functionality but also architecting the entire infrastructure stack to comply with jurisdictional requirements, often demanding data sovereignty, isolation, auditability, and robust disaster recovery scenarios. Architecture must include reusable deployment blueprints, compliance automation frameworks, observability standards, and secure environments that balance rapid expansion with stringent regulatory demands. Here, again, architecture complexity emerges directly from business goals, enabling rapid expansion into new territories while maintaining regulatory compliance and operational excellence. Data-Intensive Architectures and Personalized Experiences The shift toward personalization, recommendations, fraud detection, and other intelligent user-centric features has significantly raised the bar for handling data and analytics within modern systems. Concepts from Big Data, Data Engineering, and Machine Learning have become integral parts of system design rather than separate analytics functions. At DraftKings, personalized user experiences in the Sportsbook, Fantasy Sports, or iGaming platforms aren’t just marketing gimmicks — they directly translate into customer engagement and revenue growth. Architecture must include seamless integration of data pipelines for real-time analytics, design data lakes and warehouses that facilitate both rapid ingestion and complex querying and incorporate ML models for recommendation or fraud prevention without sacrificing performance or introducing unnecessary complexity. The need for real-time personalization — such as offering tailored betting odds based on past behavior — drives us to design systems that can handle massive data streams, continuous training and inference loops, and strong data governance. This is driven not by the availability of technology, but by the critical business need to create compelling, tailored user experiences. Architecting with Business Complexity in Mind It’s vital to underscore that architects aren’t chasing trends; rather, they leverage emerging technologies strategically to address evolving business complexity. At DraftKings, adopting microservices or event-driven designs wasn’t simply following an industry pattern — it was driven by the core need to build flexible products capable of handling massive spikes in traffic during key sports events. Similarly, embracing Kubernetes or IaC frameworks wasn’t about technological enthusiasm only; it was about rapidly deploying stable environments to support business growth and regulatory compliance. AI and ML integrations weren’t just tech showcases — they were (and will be in the future) deeply tied to delivering unique customer value, engagement, and operational excellence. Thus, the real architectural shift isn’t about any specific technology — it’s about the expanded responsibility architecture now carries: managing complexity at scale, adapting rapidly to shifting business landscapes, and ensuring that each new architectural decision directly enables business innovation rather than merely reflects technological fashion. The Architect’s Evolving Responsibilities (and Why They Aren’t Going Away) If we accept that architecture is still essential, how exactly does the architect contribute to a modern agile organization? What do they do day-to-day that a “regular” senior engineer might not? This section looks at the key responsibilities of software architects as they stand today — blending traditional expectations with new twists — and why these responsibilities are more important than ever. Strategic Technical Decision-Making and Alignment One of the architect’s foremost roles is serving as a strategic decision-maker at the intersection of technology and business. Architects possess the unique ability to see both the detailed technical landscape and the broader business goals, enabling them to make informed decisions that balance immediate product needs with long-term organizational vision. Architects often play a critical role in providing high-level estimates and making technical complexity visible and understandable to product and business stakeholders. Rather than hiding engineering complexity, they actively communicate the potential impacts of technical decisions on timelines, budgets, and resource allocation. This transparency facilitates better-informed decisions, aligning business expectations with realistic technical outcomes and mitigating misunderstandings early in the process. When initiating entirely new product lines or strategic initiatives, architects collaborate closely with product management and business leaders from the outset. Their role here is pivotal: architects help define what is technically feasible, outline potential risks, identify critical technology decisions, and ensure alignment with existing systems or broader organizational strategies. This close collaboration between architecture, product, and business teams ensures foundational decisions are sound, reducing risk and increasing confidence as new projects launch. A clear example of strategic architectural involvement is geographic or market expansion. Entering new markets or regions, especially heavily regulated ones, involves significant architectural considerations — from compliance and data sovereignty to latency management and disaster recovery strategies. Architects provide early input into these decisions, defining how systems should adapt or scale, which significantly influences timelines, cost estimations, and even the viability of expansion initiatives. Architects also play a vital role in mergers and acquisitions (M&A). Experienced senior architects often participate directly in technical due diligence processes, evaluating potential acquisitions or partnerships. They assess architectural compatibility, integration complexity, compliance concerns, and identify risks that could undermine expected synergies. Their assessments provide critical insights to business stakeholders, directly influencing deal valuation, negotiation strategy, and post-acquisition integration planning. Similarly, integrating new third-party providers, strategic partners, or suppliers involves architects from initial evaluation to final implementation. Architects evaluate the technical capabilities of partners, assess compatibility with existing systems, and define integration strategies, considering security, scalability, compliance, and maintainability. Their involvement ensures that partnerships add strategic value without introducing unforeseen technical debt or operational risks. Importantly, modern architects influence without always having direct authority. They often operate by persuasion, education, and community leadership. By clearly communicating technical vision, facilitating productive discussions, and guiding collective decision-making, architects cultivate an inclusive environment. This collaborative strategic role ensures that architecture is not a dictatorship of one brilliant mind but rather a shared vision continually refined by many, with the architect acting as its steward and champion. Embedding Quality Attributes through Strategic Collaboration A key advantage architects bring to the engineering organization is their unique ability to address quality attributes, such as security, scalability, performance, reliability, and resilience, not merely as isolated concerns but from an integrated, strategic perspective. Their vantage point, spanning multiple teams and product lines, allows them to proactively recognize shared challenges and facilitate solutions that provide lasting, reusable value. Rather than tackling quality attributes individually, architects regularly engage with Infrastructure and Platform Engineering teams to collaboratively design foundational solutions that initially address specific, urgent domain needs. These solutions, however, are strategically designed for broader applicability across multiple domains or teams in the future. Architects, therefore, bridge immediate business requirements with long-term organizational goals, ensuring efficiency and reducing redundant engineering efforts. For instance, an architect might help Infrastructure and Platform teams build a scalable, elastic infrastructure tailored initially for high-volume, real-time interactions typical in online sports betting scenarios. By ensuring the solution is flexible and generic enough to support other potential use cases, the architect maximizes organizational value beyond the immediate project. This approach reduces the future overhead of engineering teams facing similar challenges elsewhere in the organization. Moreover, architects actively cultivate a culture of knowledge sharing and continuous learning across the organization. When a successful architectural solution is developed, architects communicate and distribute these new concepts across teams. This collaboration often occurs through architecture forums, guild meetings, or documentation of best practices, enabling rapid dissemination of architectural knowledge and promoting consistency in addressing common engineering challenges. Architects’ unique organizational position — spanning multiple product teams, engineering groups, and business units — provides them with the perspective and influence required to align cross-team initiatives. By working closely with Infrastructure, Platform Engineering, and domain-specific teams, architects ensure that strategic initiatives addressing essential quality attributes remain aligned with overall organizational goals and technological direction. The key point is that architects think about risk mitigation from day one. Every system has risks: the risk of being hacked, the risk of crashing under load, the risk of data inconsistency, etc. Architects identify the major risks for the system being built and ensure the design addresses them proactively. This doesn’t mean overengineering for hypothetical scale or gold-plating everything — it’s a balance. Good architects are pragmatic;​ they gauge what level of robustness is needed for the context. This proactive, collaborative, and strategic focus on quality attributes distinguishes the architecture role from other senior engineering positions. Architects not only identify and solve technical issues as they emerge but also strategically enable the broader engineering organization to anticipate, manage, and consistently deliver high-quality, resilient, and secure systems aligned to long-term business objectives. Enabling Agility through Continuous Architectural Improvement Software architecture is often misunderstood as a static discipline, focused on planning upfront and delivering comprehensive blueprints to implementation teams. This misperception sometimes leads to the idea that architectural work conflicts with agile methods, which prioritize adaptability, iterative delivery, and rapid response to change. In reality, modern architectural practice not only aligns closely with agile methodologies — it embodies them. Architectural work is inherently an agile discipline because it is structured around systematic evaluation, continuous improvement, rapid feedback loops, and adaptability to changing requirements. Architects don’t merely respond to immediate product or engineering demands; instead, they proactively anticipate evolving business needs, evaluate potential impacts, and guide engineering teams through incremental implementation steps. This systematic yet iterative planning process ensures that the architecture remains flexible enough to accommodate future changes, thus enhancing the organization’s overall agility. Unlike the outdated perception of architecture as a detached function (the earlier mentioned “Ivory Tower”) from practical realities, contemporary architects maintain close relationships not just with engineering, but also with product management, operations, marketing, customer experience, and compliance teams. Their broad and cross-functional collaboration enables architects to stay aligned with business strategies, emerging market trends, and shifting customer expectations. This continuous dialogue across departments allows architects to integrate new insights rapidly into architectural planning, ensuring that systems remain robust, relevant, and adaptable. This doesn’t mean architectural work is spontaneous or unstructured — quite the opposite. Architecture is fundamentally an engineering discipline built on meticulous planning, systematic research, careful evaluation of trade-offs, and data-driven decision-making. Architects continuously research and evaluate new methodologies, frameworks, and technologies in advance of actual needs, enabling informed choices rather than impulsive reactions. This careful preparation means that when business priorities shift or new market opportunities emerge, architects are equipped with practical knowledge and viable options already evaluated and tested. Another critical aspect is that architects maintain an organizational view, continuously identifying patterns, reuse opportunities, and efficiency gains across multiple product domains and teams. Rather than making isolated decisions optimized for individual projects or immediate challenges, architects identify broader patterns, architectural solutions, and best practices that can be leveraged repeatedly. This structured, engineering-based approach allows the organization to scale effectively, reduce redundant efforts, and incrementally improve the overall quality of systems. Architects enable continuous improvement by incorporating agile engineering principles directly into architectural guidelines, including modular designs, loose coupling, incremental deployment strategies, experimentation, and automated testing frameworks. This ensures that architectural solutions remain practical, sustainable, and straightforward to refine and evolve. Architects consistently communicate these patterns to engineering teams, reinforcing the organization’s commitment to agility and continuous learning. In many agile frameworks, architects are explicitly recognized for their strategic value, just like product, delivery, and engineering. SAFe, for example, clearly identifies architects at multiple organizational levels (solution, system, and enterprise), and not only SAFe. Architects in these roles continuously translate high-level business objectives into actionable technical strategies and clearly articulated engineering plans. They balance strategic direction and tactical implementation, systematically steering the organization toward long-term architectural objectives while enabling agile teams to deliver incremental, measurable value in shorter cycles. The Architect–Principal Partnership: A Strategic Collaboration While this article has outlined the distinctions between Architects and Principal Engineers, it’s important to emphasize that these roles are not in competition — they are complementary and, in fact, mutually reinforcing. A future-ready engineering organization must rely on both to operate effectively, especially when navigating complexity, scale, and continuous change. At DraftKings, we embrace this duality as a core part of how we structure our architecture function. Architects and Principal Engineers collaborate tightly, forming a continuous feedback loop between high-level vision and domain-specific execution. In most cases, the architect works directly with the Principal Engineer in a given domain or vertical. When no Principal is present, that collaboration naturally shifts to the next senior engineering role — in our case, typically a Senior Lead Software Engineer. This collaborative model ensures that any architectural solution — be it for a new feature, an infrastructure upgrade, a response to technical debt, or an entirely new product line — is shaped by both a broad architectural perspective and deep local expertise. The result is not an isolated decision but a shared design process where accountability and ownership adapt to the complexity at hand. Sometimes, the Principal Engineer leads the architectural effort for their domain, with the architect serving as a consultative peer and strategic reviewer. Other times, the architect is responsible for the solution, with the Principal deeply involved throughout the process. In yet other cases, the architect might only participate in key reviews and validations, leaving the implementation details and ownership to the engineering leadership. The degree of involvement is always calibrated to the complexity and impact of what we’re trying to achieve. What makes this relationship work is not rigid definitions, but a shared understanding of purpose. Architects bring the context of the broader system, strategic alignment, and patterns that have worked elsewhere in the organization. Principals bring hands-on technical awareness, domain depth, and proximity to product and team dynamics. Both roles are essential. And it’s the dynamic interplay between them — the iterative refinement of solutions from both a strategic and tactical lens — that allows engineering organizations to scale without sacrificing coherence, velocity, or architectural quality. The architect–principal relationship is the connective tissue that holds together the layers of system design, product development, and long-term technology strategy. In a world that increasingly rewards speed, adaptability, and intelligent system composition, this relationship is no longer optional — it is foundational. Press enter or click to view image in full size From Code to Capability: The Architectural Shift Driven by AI and Abstraction We stand at an extraordinary turning point in software architecture — one catalyzed by the rise of artificial intelligence, but whose roots extend far deeper into the very essence of human-technological evolution. Throughout history, advancements in software development have consistently been marked by abstraction: each new paradigm has moved us progressively away from hardware-specific instructions and toward human-centric expression. Today, AI accelerates this evolution dramatically, pushing architects to re-envision the very definition of what constitutes a “system.” Philosophically, AI embodies a profound shift toward systems designed around human intentions rather than lines of code. AI-driven technologies — ranging from generative coding assistants to autonomous AI agents capable of decision-making, planning, and direct interaction with users — represent an unprecedented elevation in our level of technological abstraction. This abstraction fundamentally transforms our architectural mindset: we are no longer constrained by the granular details of implementations, but instead think in terms of orchestrating intelligent capabilities that closely mirror human reasoning and intent. In this new paradigm, architects serve as the critical link between abstract human objectives and the increasingly sophisticated technological landscape, carefully aligning powerful yet opaque intelligent capabilities with strategic business goals and human values. This evolution provokes a deep reconsideration of the architect’s role. Traditionally, architects bridged human needs with technical implementations, turning business requirements into actionable system designs. Today, as AI and intelligent automation blur distinctions between human cognitive processes and technological execution, architects face an exciting but daunting responsibility: shaping software systems composed not merely of code or algorithms but of intelligent capabilities and behaviors themselves. Architects must grapple philosophically with unprecedented questions: How do we govern the ethics of intelligent systems? How do we ensure explainability and accountability when parts of the system are no longer entirely under human comprehension or control? How do we preserve human agency in an AI-enabled system landscape? These questions define the new frontier for software architecture, requiring architects to become not just technical leaders, but thought leaders — active participants in shaping the future relationship between humans and intelligent technologies. Yet this philosophical evolution brings equally profound practical implications. As architects begin thinking at the level of intelligent capabilities, their approach shifts concretely toward solution-centric, composable architectures. Architects increasingly operate as curators and integrators, assembling solutions from pre-existing modules, intelligent services, AI components, third-party APIs, and internally developed systems. Rather than building from scratch, architects now define interfaces, establish contracts, and create modular structures that allow components to be combined and recombined flexibly. This practical shift profoundly influences existing architectural methodologies and patterns: loose coupling, event-driven designs, modularity, and clear contracts become much more essential, ensuring that the overall architecture remains stable and adaptable as individual capabilities evolve. In the composable enterprise, architecture practice shifts from specifying detailed technical implementations to ensuring the coherence, interoperability, and resilience of solutions built from diverse components. Architects establish strategic guardrails and standards, such as common API structures, unified integration patterns, and consistent observability mechanisms, to allow rapid yet controlled evolution. The role of architecture extends to curating internal marketplaces or catalogs of reusable capabilities, which teams leverage to quickly and reliably assemble new solutions. Architects themselves become active participants in the continuous evaluation and improvement of this catalog, guiding strategic investment into reusable components or capabilities aligned with long-term organizational goals. Moreover, architects will (if not already) face an expanded set of responsibilities that extend into ethical and sustainable considerations. Intelligent technologies pose ethical questions related to data usage, privacy, transparency, and accountability. Architects — uniquely positioned at the intersection of technology, business, and user experience — must proactively establish architectural frameworks that address these concerns. This broader ethical and social perspective is yet to be unpacked, but it will elevate architecture from purely technical considerations to genuine stewardship of organizational values and societal impact. This evolution reflects well on the true purpose of the architectural role: shaping the relationship between humanity and technology. As the level of abstraction rises, architects, ever pragmatic yet visionary, are transforming from code-centric toward capability-centric thinking, driven by AI and abstraction. Philosophically, architects must grapple with AI’s ethical and human implications, practically, they must adopt composable, modular patterns to rapidly assemble reliable solutions aligned to strategic business goals. Press enter or click to view image in full size Architecting the Future Organization: Toward Continuous Architectural Excellence at DraftKings As software architecture continues its evolution toward higher abstraction, intelligent capabilities, and solution-centric design, traditional ways of structuring architectural practices must be reconsidered. At DraftKings, architecture is no longer purely a technical function, isolated into a single team, or tied solely to specific domains. Instead, we’ve consciously structured architecture as a strategic capability embedded throughout the organization, designed deliberately to support agility, abstraction, and continuous improvement. Future-ready architectural structures rely less on rigid hierarchical lines and more on carefully orchestrated interactions among different types of architectural expertise. Within DraftKings, we’ve intentionally chosen clear yet flexible terminology — Embedded Architects and Global Architects — to avoid restrictive definitions like “Enterprise Architect,” “Systems Architect,” or specific frameworks such as SAFe’s predefined architectural roles. This deliberate simplicity aligns perfectly with our philosophy: maintaining flexibility and adaptability within the architectural function itself. Domain-Embedded Architects at DraftKings Our embedded architects maintain deep, ongoing relationships within defined business or technical domains. Their role balances stability and responsiveness, focused on translating evolving product and business needs into clear architectural pathways. Rather than designing solutions in isolation, embedded architects engage daily with product owners, engineers, operational teams, and stakeholders from various functions. Their continuous involvement allows them to proactively shape the architectural “runway” ahead of immediate product demands, ensuring architectural changes happen just in time rather than reactively. Embedded architects serve as trusted experts and mentors within their domains, embedding strategic architectural thinking directly into the teams responsible for delivering software. Global Cross-Domain Architects at DraftKings Complementing embedded architects are our global architects, strategically positioned to operate at a higher level of abstraction and across multiple domains. Their role isn’t bound to specific product lines but spans horizontally across the entire organization. Global architects lead strategic, cross-functional initiatives such as mergers and acquisitions, major product integrations, long-term technology evaluations, and partnerships, guiding DraftKings through complex decisions involving multiple business units, technological ecosystems, and external providers. These architects maintain a future-oriented perspective, continuously scanning the technology landscape for emerging trends and proactively integrating them into our broader architectural vision. Together, embedded and global architects create a dynamic interplay that effectively bridges immediate tactical needs and long-term strategic goals. Global architects leverage deep domain insights provided by embedded architects to inform high-level strategic direction, while embedded architects draw on global architects’ broader perspectives to anticipate shifts and proactively adopt innovative architectural solutions. The Capability Marketplace: Architecting Through Composable Capabilities In this forward-looking architectural organization, the internal capability marketplace concept emerges as a central, defining innovation. Rather than limiting architecture to the specification of technical details and prescriptive designs, architects curate and maintain an internal marketplace of reusable and composable software capabilities. Each capability represents a cohesive, abstracted solution or intelligent functionality that teams can integrate seamlessly into their products, ranging from intelligent decision-making components powered by AI to standardized modules for security, compliance, or personalization. The capability marketplace embodies the architectural shift from code-centric implementation to capability-oriented abstraction. It allows architects to manage complexity, maintain consistency, and enable rapid innovation simultaneously. Architects oversee the marketplace, setting strategic guidelines for interoperability, quality standards, security considerations, and ethical usage policies. Teams across the organization benefit from easy access to trusted, reusable capabilities that accelerate delivery and ensure architectural coherence without sacrificing creativity or autonomy. Architectural governance in this model moves away from top-down enforcement and toward collaborative stewardship. Architects no longer solely control the architectural landscape but instead guide and empower product teams, helping them navigate strategic trade-offs, integrate complex capabilities, and adopt emerging technologies responsibly. This form of governance ensures that as the technology ecosystem continuously evolves, the organization remains capable of integrating new capabilities rapidly and sustainably. To be candid, DraftKings is very far from implementing such a capability marketplace. However, this type of theoretical idealism and forward-thinking is precisely what drives our architectural vision. It’s this ambition and clarity of direction that gives me confidence that we will indeed reach this future. Conclusion: Architects as Visionaries in an Age of Abstraction At the heart of this article lies a fundamental truth: the essence of software architecture has always been about connecting human intent to technical realities. Historically, this connection was tangible, bound tightly to lines of code and physical infrastructures. Today, it is abstracted by layering concepts, API-Led architectures, and other patterns. Tomorrow, it will become more fluid and increasingly mediated by intelligent systems, forcing us to rethink what it means to architect at all. The redefinition of titles from “Architect” to roles like Principal or Staff Engineer does not diminish the essential need for architectural thinking — if anything, it intensifies it. In a technology landscape now defined by unprecedented intelligent abstraction and a constantly growing business appetite, organizations neglecting dedicated, strategic architectural oversight risk fragmentation, inefficiency, and chaos. Titles aside, it is the explicit investment of time, energy, and thought into a holistic, strategic system design that distinguishes enduring companies from those perpetually caught in cycles of technical debt and reactive firefighting. The advent of AI, intelligent automation, and composable capabilities is not merely another technological shift — it signals a profound philosophical transition. Architects of today and tomorrow must navigate increasingly abstract environments, orchestrating systems composed of intelligent, autonomous capabilities rather than code alone. The challenge lies in understanding and guiding this new relationship between product requirements and technological potential, maintaining clarity amid the rising complexity and abstraction. Architecting systems that gracefully integrate intelligent agents and dynamic capabilities is no longer simply a technical skill — it’s a visionary practice, reflecting our understanding of how technology should seamlessly empower human intent. This understanding shapes the way I approach building and leading architectural organizations today. I actively pursue flexibility, resisting rigid categorizations, because I believe future-ready architecture demands adaptability above all else. Architecting capabilities (vs. implementing a feature) is the guiding star that continuously motivates me to innovate not only within the products I deliver but also fundamentally in how I conceive and structure engineering itself. Let this article serve not as a conclusion, but as an opening statement in an ongoing conversation. My hope is to ignite curiosity, inspire deeper inquiry, and encourage architects and technology leaders alike to rethink and refine the way we practice architecture. The road ahead is indeed uncertain, but filled with extraordinary potential for those willing to reimagine the role of architects as strategic visionaries, capable of thoughtfully guiding our collective journey into a future shaped by continuous change and boundless innovation.

title: Kodiak Selects Roush as Manufacturing Partner to Upfit Kodiak Driver-Equipped Trucks
summary: Kodiak AI partners with Roush to scale upfitting of autonomous trucks, enabling broader deployment of Kodiak Driver-powered vehicles starting in late 2025.
body_text: Kodiak expects its collaboration with Roush will enable it to scale the deployment of Kodiak Driver-equipped trucks beginning in the second half of 2025 MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif. and LIVONIA, Mich. — Kodiak AI, Inc. ("Kodiak”), a leading provider of AI-powered autonomous vehicle technology, and Roush Industries, Inc. (“Roush”), a leading product development supplier serving the mobility, aerospace, defense, and theme park industries, today announced that the companies will work together to scale upfitting of autonomous trucks equipped with the Kodiak Driver, Kodiak’s advanced AI-powered autonomous solution. Starting in the second half of 2025, Roush will upfit these trucks in its facility in Livonia, Michigan. The first trucks Roush will upfit are expected to be for Kodiak’s customer, Atlas Energy Solutions (NYSE: AESI), as Kodiak and Atlas work to expand the driverless operations they began in December 2024. In collaboration with Kodiak, Roush has committed to open a production line for scaled upfitting of trucks equipped with the Kodiak Driver’s modular and vehicle-agnostic hardware. This hardware includes Kodiak’s proprietary SensorPods, AI compute, Actuation Control Engine safety compute, and redundant actuation elements. Roush has also committed to design, develop and implement a flexible manufacturing process that can rapidly scale as Kodiak increases its upfit of Kodiak Driver-powered trucks to meet customer demand. “Kodiak’s autonomous trucking technology is an exciting advancement in the mobility industry,” said Brad Rzetelny, VP Contract Manufacturing, Roush. “Together we’re working to build a robust and repeatable manufacturing process that supports Kodiak’s transition from limited production to full-scale deployment. Kodiak’s technology and engineering rigor set a high bar, and we believe we are uniquely positioned to meet that bar at scale.” For nearly 50 years Roush has been a trusted name in mobility. Today, the company is recognized as a highly-regarded provider of product development services which includes systems integration, manufacturing, and modification services. Roush has developed deep expertise in upfitting and delivering complex vehicles, including autonomous vehicles for multiple developers. The company’s demonstrated track record of bringing innovative products to market establishes a strong foundation for Kodiak to scale the deployment of the Kodiak Driver. “Roush’s deep experience upfitting autonomous vehicles makes them an ideal production partner for Kodiak,” said Don Burnette, Founder and CEO, Kodiak. “We believe that Roush’s strong quality management processes will ensure our customers’ Kodiak Driver-powered trucks will be built to exacting standards, while giving us the manufacturing flexibility to support a wide range of vehicle configurations, including different vehicle and cab types, axle setups, and heavy-duty applications to meet the diverse demands of the trucking industry. Unlike traditional factory-line integration, which is limited to a single configuration, we believe that working with Roush will allow us to move faster and customize vehicles to meet customer needs.” In December 2024, Kodiak became the first publicly announced company to deliver driverless semi-trucks to a customer. In April, Kodiak announced it is seeking to go public through a business combination with Ares Acquisition Corporation II (NYSE: AACT). The proposed business combination is expected to close in the second half of 2025, subject to approval by AACT and Kodiak stockholders and the satisfaction or waiver of customary closing conditions. Upon the closing of the proposed business combination, the combined company is expected to be listed on a national stock exchange. By partnering with AACT and accessing the public markets, Kodiak intends to accelerate its go-to-market strategy, meet growing customer demand, tackle critical industry challenges and unlock the trucking industry’s estimated $4+ trillion global market opportunity. About Kodiak AI, Inc. Kodiak AI, Inc. was founded in 2018 and is a leading provider of AI-powered autonomous vehicle technology that is designed to help tackle some of the toughest driving jobs. Kodiak’s driverless solution can help address the critical problem of safely transporting goods in the face of unprecedented supply chain challenges. Kodiak’s vision is to become the trusted world leader in autonomous ground transportation. Kodiak is committed to a safer and more efficient future for all through the commercialization of driverless trucking at scale. To that end, Kodiak developed the Kodiak Driver, a virtual driver that combines advanced AI-powered software with modular and vehicle-agnostic hardware designed to help address Kodiak’s customers’ needs. The Kodiak Driver is not just an idea—it is operating without a human driver today. Kodiak serves customers in both commercial trucking and the public sector. In 2024, Kodiak believes it achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first company to deploy customer-owned and -operated driverless trucks in commercial service. The Kodiak Driver is also being utilized in the public sector, where Kodiak believes it can support national security initiatives and critical government applications. About Roush For close to 50 years, Roush has boldly imagined and created remarkable solutions for some of the world's greatest organizations. We dream, design, engineer, test, and deliver extraordinary products for customers in the advanced mobility, aerospace, defense, and theme park industries. Roush is unique in its ability to leverage services across the complete product development cycle, solving customers' most complex challenges and accelerating critical product launch targets.

title: Go Big or Go Home: The Benefits of CommScope® OM4 Deep Lid Nodes
summary: CommScopes new deep lid housing form factor supports a variety of network technologies to provide operators with flexibility and performance.
body_text: Go Big or Go Home: The Benefits of CommScope® OM4 Deep Lid Nodes CommScope’s new deep lid housing form factor supports a variety of network technologies to provide operators with flexibility and performance. Author David Musser Product Line Manager, ANS Business Strategy See all posts by this author Published June 23, 2025 7 minute read Share Categories CCAP DOCSIS Access network cabling and connectivity Many cable operators still run HFC cable access networks at sub-split frequencies; CommScope estimates that approximately 80% of Converged Cable Access Platforms (CCAPs) currently in operation support full DOCSIS® 3.1 operation, but only 30% of them currently operate with mid-split or high-split networks. Operators who are currently still operating sub-split networks haven’t begun to unlock the full potential of their network assets—nor have they laid the foundation for the transition to next-generation network technologies such as DAA or Node PON. But with the advent of new, next-generation technologies, which support increased bandwidth, throughput speeds and capacities, many cable operators have already begun the process of modernizing their networks to improve performance and lay the groundwork for next-generation technology deployments. This process often raises concerns over “regret spending”—investing in current technology, only to have it supplanted in a few years by more-advanced or better-performing products, requiring new expenditures to upgrade recently-purchased equipment. To address this concern, CommScope has developed a “deep” lid version of its Opti Max® OM4 and NC4000® optical node series. The deep lid variant is an economical option for both optimizing current HFC network performance and paving the way for future deployments of next-generation technologies. Current investments in these nodes can help improve network performance now and still retain their value as new technologies come to market in the future. The deep lid form factor supports a variety of network technologies not currently supported by standard lid OM4 housings, from optimized D3.1 Enhanced (D3.1 E ) high-split network operation to next-generation Distributed Access Architecture (DAA) and Node PON technologies. Cable operators can choose one of two deep lid options: a factory-configured deep lid OM4 series node or an upgrade kit that enables field technicians to modify fielded, standard-lid OM4 nodes with deep lids. This flexibility helps cable operators choose the deep lid option which best suits their budgets and upgrade plans. The deep lid explained Standard lid OM4 housings have a total of depth of ~10 inches. This depth of housing supports the form factor of previous generation OM4-style and NC4-style analog and digital transmitters and receivers. OM4 deep lid housings, on the other hand, have a total depth of ~11.4 inches; this added depth supports the form factors of a wider variety of CommScope’s node-based modules: NC4-style receivers and transceivers in OM4 deep lid housings, DAA modules, and Node PON modules. The deep lid, therefore, provides cable operators with support for a wider range of network upgrade options than the standard lid. The deep lid design also features improved heat dissipation to further support future power-hungry applications such as Node PON. Deep lids also support an NC4-style high-performance, high-efficiency power supply, designed specifically to support the powering requirements of DAA modules. The deep lid and optimized HFC access network performance Since many cable operators will choose a mid-split or high-split plant upgrade as the quickest and most-cost effective way of optimizing their current plants, they can choose to deploy deep lid nodes in one of two DOCSIS HFC access split upgrade scenarios: To transition from sub-split to mid-split operation as an intermediate step toward an eventual high-split plant upgrade To support a mid-split to high-split plant upgrade Either option supports enhanced network operation strategies that can unlock the latent speeds and capacities available in current HFC cable access networks. While standard lids support mid-split digital return operation and high-split analog return operation, the DT4600—CommScope’s high-split digital return transceiver—can only be installed in a deep lid form factor in OM4 series nodes (NC4 series nodes already support the DT4600 form factor). Therefore, cable operators using standard lid OM4 nodes in a current mid-split plant with digital return, but who have plans to upgrade the plant for high-split operation, can install deep lid nodes with DT4600 return transceivers to continue operating at mid-split frequencies; they can then seamlessly transition to high-split operation when they are ready without installing new digital return transceivers. Access to DOCSIS 3.1 E performance Cable operators can also leverage a mid-split or high-split deep lid node deployment to support the roll-out of DOCSIS 3.1 Enhanced (D3.1 E ) technology. D3.1 E can significantly enhance downstream speeds and capacities with minimally invasive changes to a current network. D3.1 E does this by expanding the maximum OFDM capacity of a mid-split or high-split network from two to four OFDM channel blocks (with SC-QAM channels) or five OFDM channel blocks (without SC-QAM channels). D3.1 E retains support for a maximum of two OFDMA channel blocks in a high-split upstream path, with throughput speeds of ~1.7 Gbps in the upstream. Besides the plant upgrade and deep lid node deployment, D3.1 E requirements are minimal: a CMTS software upgrade in the headend—Software Release 13 and higher for E6000® CERs, Software Release v8.12 and higher for C100G CMTS chassis—and targeted deployments of next-generation DOCSIS® 3.1+ or DOCSIS 4.0 CPEs to support D3.1 E ’s expanded OFDM capacity. Full D3.1 E operation—i.e., mid-split or high-split operation without SC-QAM channels—can provide throughput speeds of up to ~8 Gbps in the downstream. Deploying D3.1 E technology in conjunction with a plant upgrade and a deep lid node installation is an excellent way for cable operators to monetize their existing network assets without significant capital expenditures or invasive network construction. D3.1 E technology can also bridge the transition from traditional HFC Access Network operation to next-generation DAA or Node PON network designs, while supporting multi-gigabit services over an existing delivery system in the interim. The deep lid and next-generation networks CommScope deep lid nodes enable cable operators to upgrade to mid-split or high-split HFC cable access network operation today, while also preparing for future DAA and/or Node PON deployments. The transition from HFC to one of these two technologies is simple and cost-effective, as the following upgrade scenarios demonstrate. Upgrade lid for 1x1, 1x2, or 2x2 DAA operation : In this upgrade scenario, a field technician will remove the NC4-style optical modules from the lid of a fielded deep lid node, remove the HFC/RPD adapter plate, and install a CommScope RD2322 RxD module. The RD2322 supports either Remote PHY and Remote MACPHY operation based on the module’s software configuration. Cable operators can install software options that support 1x1, 1x2, or 2x2 segmentation from a single RD2322 module. Upgrade lid for DAA operation with expanded upstream segmentation : In this upgrade scenario, a field technician will remove the NC4-style optical modules from the lid of a fielded deep lid node and replace the optical modules with a CommScope RD1424-M4 module. The RD1424-M4 supports Remote PHY operation only. Cable operators can configure up to two downstream and up to four upstream segments without the need for software upgrades. Upgrade lid for Node PON operation : In this upgrade scenario, a field technician will install a CommScope XE4202M R-OLT or XP4202 XGS-PON Remote OLT (R-OLT) Module on the right side of the HFC/RPD adapter plate, leaving the NC4-style optical modules in place on the left side of the adapter plate. This node configuration supports up to two downstream receivers and two upstream transmitters for a maximum 2x2 segmentation. The XP4202 XGX-PON R-OLT module supports high bandwidth ITU GPON/XGS-PON based services, while the XE4202M R-OLT supports IEEE EPON/10G EPON based services. By leveraging an existing HFC deep lid node installation, cable operators can significantly reduce future spends for DAA or Node PON deployments. Even if they choose to go directly from standard lid HFC operation to deep lid DAA or Node PON deployments, they can still realize a cost benefit by simply upgrading the node in the future with new DAA or Node PON modules as they come to market, rather than rebuying a new node. Conclusion CommScope’s OM4 series deep lid nodes support both stages of a cable operator’s network evolution, enabling cable operators to increase average revenue per user (ARPU) and keep pace with their competitors, while all but eliminating regret spending as networks continue to evolve. With game-changing technologies such as D3.1 E , DAA, and Node PON available now, it’s the perfect time for cable operators to consider deep lid upgrades for their OM4 series nodes. title: How to Sell a Condo in Singapore (2026 Guide)
summary: Looking to sell your condo with a property agent? Here's a guide to help you navigate the whole process so you won't get lost during your transaction journey.
body_text: Last Updated on June 25, 2026 by Yolly Del Prado TL;DR / Summary: – Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD) applies if you sell within 4 years of purchase (up to 16% tax); no SSD is payable after 4 years. -Before listing, estimate your condo’s value and calculate potential cash proceeds after fees, taxes, and legal costs to understand your real returns. -Sellers must grant an Option to Purchase (OTP) , which becomes legally binding once the buyer exercises it and pays the deposit. -The buyer typically pays a 1% option fee first, followed by about 4% upon exercising the OTP , before the sale proceeds to legal completion. The process of selling a private property, such as a condo, in Singapore involves checking whether Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD) applies, pricing your unit based on recent transactions, preparing it for viewings, granting an Option to Purchase (OTP), and completing the legal transfer with your lawyer. While there are generally fewer restrictions when selling a condo compared to selling an HDB flat , the timeline, documentation, and financial calculations still require careful planning. In this guide, we’ll walk you through each step clearly so you know what to expect and how to confidently navigate your condo sale. Step-by-step Guide to Sell Your Condo: 1. Check Payable Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD) 2. Conduct Market Research and Post Condo Listing 3. Home Staging and Renovation 4. Get Matched to Your Ideal Buyer 5. Arrange Viewings and Negotiations 6. Contact a Lawyer and Grant the Option to Purchase 7. Buyer to Exercise OTP 8. Complete the Sale Ready to Sell Your Condo? Get in Touch With the Top 1% of Agents in Singapore Frequently Asked Questions About Selling Condo in Singapore 1. Check Payable Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD) The first thing to determine when selling your condo is whether Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD) applies based on how long you’ve owned the property. If you have owned your condo for more than 4 years , no SSD is payable. You may proceed directly to Step 2. If you are selling within 4 years of purchase , SSD will apply based on your holding period. SSD applies to private residential properties, including condos, that are sold within the first 4 years of ownership under Singapore’s property cooling measures. This is the minimum holding period, similar to the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP ) for HDB flats, that requires you to physically stay in your condo before you’re eligible to sell. If SSD applies, payment must be made within 14 days from the date the Option to Purchase (OTP) is exercised. The tax is calculated based on the higher of the selling price or market value. SSD Rates From 4 July 2025 Onwards Holding Period SSD Payable (% of actual price/market value) Up to 1 year 16% More than 1 year and up to 2 years 12% More than 2 years and up to 3 years 8% More than 3 years and up to 4 years 4% More than 4 years No SSD Payable 2. Conduct Market Research and Post Condo Listing Before putting your condo up for sale, you’ll want to get a rough idea of how much other condos in your area have been transacted for, so you can keep your asking price reasonable while also ensuring that you don’t get ripped off by an opportunistic buyer. To aid your market research, you can use HomerAI to check your condo’s estimated value for free. Simply enter your address to get an instant valuation and a clearer understanding of your potential sale proceeds before listing your unit. Along with your estimated value, you can also view recent condo transactions in your area, calculate your expected cash proceeds after deducting costs such as SSD, legal fees and agent commissions, and use the affordability calculator to assess how much you can budget for your next property purchase. 3. Home Staging and Renovation To give yourself the best chance of selling your condo at the best price, you’ll want to put your best foot forward. There’s a name for this: home staging. Rearrange your existing furniture, declutter your living and dining areas, as well as your rooms and bathrooms, to present a clean and organised home. This will help potential buyers visualise themselves living in your home. If you engage us to sell your condo, our Super Agents will guide you on what kind of staging your home needs. Now, you might be tempted to renovate your home to negotiate a higher selling price. Instead of forking out extra cash for a full home makeover, you should repair all your lighting fixtures, doorknobs, and bathroom fixtures instead. You can also consider adding more electrical points in key areas of the home, such as beside sofas and beds, to accommodate your buyers’ lifestyle of working from home or lounging at night while charging their phones. 4. Get Matched to Your Ideal Buyer After preparing and listing your condo, the next step is finding a suitable buyer. While property portals help create visibility, a successful sale often depends on reaching buyers who are already searching for a condo with similar location, budget, and preferences. To support this, Ohmyhome uses MATCH , an algorithm that propels accurate buyer matches and supercharges your home sale. In fact, we are able to transact properties at 11x faster than the industry average with the help of this technology. With over 200,000 monthly active users, MATCH functions as a powerful aggregator to generate the most number of buyers for you. We’ll send your condo listing for sale to buyers who are looking for a property like yours; after which, all you have to do is select the best candidate for your home. If you’re looking to buy a condo and found this article, you can let us know what property you’re looking for by filling up this form , and we’ll send you all available listings directly to your WhatsApp. 5. Arrange Viewings and Negotiations Your asking price is not the final transaction price. Buyers will throw curveballs at you to bring the price down, which you must be ready to counter if you wish to get your ideal profit. Negotiations will definitely put your market research to the test. You’ll want to have looked at the properties within a 1km radius of your home , as well as the recent transactions in your area, which you can find on HomerAI . This will give you hard, concrete numbers to fall back on when buyers quote a price below the market rate. That said, there’s only so much groundwork the average person can do. With a property agent on your side, you can rely on their negotiation skills and market knowledge to secure the best price for your condo. 6. Contact a Lawyer and Grant the Option to Purchase At this stage, you’ll need to engage a lawyer to draft the terms and conditions in the Option to Purchase (OTP) and prepare the necessary documents for the transfer of ownership. Unlike OTPs for HDB flats, which can be downloaded from the HDB website, OTPs for private properties have to be drafted by a lawyer or an agent authorised to handle legal documents relating to property. Once the OTP has been drafted, the buyer can proceed with the purchase from you at 1% of your condo selling price. That’s the Option Fee, which can be negotiated. The Option Fee is there to simply lock down the buyer’s offer. You will then have to sign the OTP once the Option Fee has been agreed upon, which will commence the Option Period. This period typically lasts between 2 to 10 weeks, depending on how negotiations go. The buyer can then decide to exercise the OTP within the 14-week Option Period, indicating his/her decision to purchase your property. 7. Buyer to Exercise OTP You don’t have to do anything at this stage except wait for the buyer to exercise the OTP. Your legal representative will inform you once it has been done. The Exercise Fee is usually 4% of the selling price and will be paid to the conveyancing account of your law firm (unless a separate private arrangement has been agreed upon between you and the buyer). You will then enter into a Sale and Purchase Agreement (S&P) with the buyer. Do remember that if the buyer does not wish to proceed with the purchase of your home and does not exercise the OTP within the stipulated 14-week Option period, the Option Fee will be forfeited. 8. Complete the Sale If you’ve engaged a lawyer or a property agent for the sale of your condo, the rest of the process should be smooth sailing from here on out. You will be required to sign documents on the final sale date and hand over your keys to the buyer. Just be sure to move out before the transfer of ownership. If you have to extend your stay beyond the date of transfer, private arrangements should be agreed upon prior to the condo sale’s completion. Ready to Sell Your Condo ? Get in Touch With the Top 1% of Agents in Singapore If you want assistance navigating the entire process of selling a condo, or any other private property, simply drop us a message on WhatsApp or talk to us via our Live Chat at the bottom, right-hand corner of the screen.
